model: 11 candidates; known per-target count 0,1,2; total<=11; each candidate belongs to at most one target; binary subset/count queries

fixed4_binary_code_bound.scope: Nonadaptive binary subset questions; distinct candidate codewords; unordered pairs of two different candidates; member count is known, so single/pair cross-cardinality collisions are irrelevant

single_pair_adaptive_lower_bound.proof: Every first subset leaves at least 28 pairs in one branch; each subsequent query returns at most three counts, so three remaining queries distinguish at most 27 pairs
single_pair_adaptive_lower_bound.other_targets: All other targets have zero members, so supply no extra membership-dependent responses
single_pair_adaptive_lower_bound.scope: Adaptive binary subset/count questions, including team-specific padding; not an impossibility theorem for arbitrary multi-level confidence submissions or other returned channels

balanced_all_single_fixed4.mean_score_domain: 24 rare rows, 11 candidate rows and 13 known negative rows; TPR at FPR .01; unrounded mean; known per-target counts
balanced_all_single_fixed4.target_policy: Assign M in ascending positive-target ID order; keep M and the four candidate subsets fixed
balanced_all_single_fixed4.scope: Every all-single type (a,0), 1<=a<=11, and every compatible disjoint individual assignment; this is a new fixed-four code, not deletion of one bit from the actually used fixed-five code

type_classification_by_proved_bounds.scope: Targets may use different four fixed binary subsets; full per-target count responses are granted, a stronger observation than their average
type_classification_by_proved_bounds.local_fiber_proof: Fix the memberships of all targets except one two-member target. They consume m-2 candidates, leaving 11-(m-2)=13-m choices. Any nonadaptive four-query policy gives these choices binary four-bit words. A duplicate word yields a pair collision; otherwise the Sidon maximum seven implies a collision whenever 13-m>=8. Keep all other memberships fixed to obtain two disjoint legal full assignments with identical responses to every query
type_classification_by_proved_bounds.stronger_embedding_proof: Choose one two-member target before fixing the other memberships. If its eleven words repeat, add any common third candidate to the two repeated words to obtain two pairs with equal sums and a three-candidate union. If all words differ, the exact Sidon maximum seven gives two colliding pairs with a four-candidate union. For m<=9, assign the other m-2 candidates identically outside that union: at least seven candidates are available. All other targets then have the same memberships and thus the same responses even when they use different questions. Every query's complete per-target responses and the average are equal
type_classification_by_proved_bounds.local_fiber_only_condition: b>0 and m<=5 (six types); subsumed by the stronger twenty-type embedding bound
type_classification_by_proved_bounds.why_not_an_adaptive_fiber_proof: In an adaptive policy the pair-target questions may change after earlier answers; one fixed four-bit code does not represent all paths

complete_common_fixed4_classification.scope: All targets use the same four fixed binary candidate subsets; target-specific padding may differ. Full per-target counts are granted. This is distinct from four fixed team-specific subsets and from adaptive search
complete_common_fixed4_classification.unique_codewords_necessary: For m<=10, put one of two equal-code candidates in a target and leave the other unassigned, then exchange them while fixing all other memberships. For m=11, put them in distinct targets and exchange them. Such target positions always exist because every target has at most two members. Thus any universally identifying common codebook must have eleven distinct words
complete_common_fixed4_classification.why_collision_pairs_disjoint: Cancelling a shared codeword from x+y=x+z would give y=z, contrary to distinct codewords
complete_common_fixed4_classification.counterexample_template_1: For b>=1 and m<=9, put colliding pair X or Y in one two-member target. Assign the other m-2 members identically from the seven candidates outside X union Y. The unused alternative pair changes no other target response
complete_common_fixed4_classification.counterexample_template_2: For b>=2 and m in {10,11}, put disjoint colliding pairs X,Y in two two-member targets and swap them. Assign the other m-4 members identically from the remaining seven candidates
complete_common_fixed4_classification.positive_template: b=0 uses the distinct four-bit singleton code. For (a,b)=(8,1),(9,1), recover the eight/nine singleton targets first; then recover the pair among the remaining three/two candidates
complete_common_fixed4_classification.positive_average_encoder: Use the existing injective type-specific M certificate; each new four-query subset selects exactly five candidates, so the same score formula and 13-negative padding remain applicable

complete_common_fixed4_classification.no_adaptive_inference: UNSAT here does not establish adaptive UNSAT; adaptive (0,1) is proved separately by the first-branch bound

target_permutation_symmetry: For known counts, zero targets can be removed and targets permuted together with their queries, M values, and decoded responses. Type-level feasibility is invariant; labelled target positions need not be re-enumerated. Real queries still map the canonical targets back to their labelled IDs
non_claims: No universal four-query guarantee: type (0,1) disproves it in this count-query model
Unknown classifications are not impossibility results
